title: A solid-state theory for dense cylindrical packings of balls
authors: Luke K. Davis, Alexander R. Klotz
abstract: We develop an analytical theory for the dense packing of hard spheres in cylinders. Physically, our theory consists of a finite cylindrical masking of a close-packed three-dimensional solid and covers the entire range of cylinder aspect ratios, thus going beyond efforts that are focused on very tall cylinders in a narrow range of widths. We explicitly derive an exact equation for resulting packing fractions, valid for any regular lattice, and it provides a basis to understand the oscillations and scaling of volume fractions that have appeared in previous works. Our analytical relation serves as a rigorous lower bound and to tighten it we derive, and implement, an efficient mathematical procedure to optimize the orientation of the cylinder. Furthermore, we suggest simple techniques to improve on the predicted packings. Overall, we provide a general theoretical foundation for the packing of balls in cylinders, valid for all container sizes.
summary: This paper provides a comprehensive analytical theory for determining the maximum packing fraction of hard spheres inside a cylinder. It establishes a rigorous lower bound using lattice masking and improves this bound through systematic optimization and the addition of 'sheaths.' The work is significant for providing a general theoretical framework applicable across all cylinder sizes.
main_problem: The paper develops an analytical theory to calculate the dense packing fraction of hard spheres (balls) confined within a cylinder, covering all aspect ratios.
main_result: The authors derive an exact analytical lower bound for the packing fraction using a lattice-masking approach, and further improve this bound using an Optimized Cylinder Orientation (OCO) procedure and a 'sheathing' construction.
method: The methods involve deriving the packing fraction using Fourier transforms of the cylindrical indicator function, optimizing the cylinder orientation via gradient conditions, and geometrically constructing successive annular sheaths.
model_or_system: The system is monodisperse hard spheres packed inside a cylinder of specified diameter and height. The theory models the packing by assuming the spheres adhere to a perfect crystal lattice (FCC or HCP).
key_observables: Packing fraction ($\phi$), which exhibits oscillatory (step-like) behavior as a function of cylinder dimensions.
important_parameters: Cylinder diameter ($2R$), cylinder height ($H$), and sphere diameter ($\sigma$). The analysis covers regimes from narrow to wide cylinders.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the packing can be modeled by masking a finite volume from a perfect, regular crystal lattice. Later derivations assume $H \gg R_0$ for sheath calculations.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the masking process, compare predicted packing fractions (lower bound vs. numerical data) across varying dimensions, and detail the geometric construction of added annular sheaths.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from establishing the basic lattice-based lower bound via Fourier analysis to introducing optimization techniques (OCO) to tighten this bound, and finally detailing a recursive 'sheathing' construction to further improve the predicted density.
why_interesting: While focused on classical geometry, the rigorous development of analytical bounds and optimization procedures for confined systems mirrors techniques used in analyzing quantum confinement effects or calculating ground state energies in geometrically constrained quantum systems.
